entries.title: Move on directional clarity.
entries.text: Organisations that cannot move until the strategy is fully documented, fully risk-assessed and fully agreed will always be slower than the environment they are trying to navigate. Move on directional clarity and fill in the detail as you go.
entries.after: Stale assumptions compound until the organisation is blindsided.

entries.title: Rigid mental models.
entries.text: People misread what is in front of them when they are held by old assumptions. Leaders who are too attached to what they already believe can miss the very signal that could renew the organisation.
entries.after: under-invest in genuinely uncomfortable questions.

entries.title: Succession of story.
entries.text: The story of how relationships were built, why systems exist and what sacrifices created the current position is one of the most undervalued strategic assets an organisation holds. When leadership changes without deliberate knowledge transfer, the organisation loses the context that makes its position intelligible. Build succession of story alongside succession of role.
entries.after: leaves, the capability collapses.

entries.title: Short-term relief, long-term cost.
entries.text: Decisions made under temporary pressure, to solve an immediate pain point at the cost of a long-term asset, are among the most damaging an organisation can make. Build a decision protocol for moments of pressure that forces long-term consideration before short-term relief is chosen.
entries.after: ecosystem relationships that make value durable.

entries.title: The party with no leverage.
entries.text: The long-term durability of an enterprise is shaped by what its most powerful actor chooses to do for the people who cannot negotiate: the junior employee, the smaller supplier, the customer with no leverage. Strategies that optimise only for the strong corrode the moral capital leaders need to lead willing teams. Audit one pending decision for what it does for the most vulnerable party in the room.
entries.after: each becomes a structural risk.

entries.title: Adapt the method, keep the purpose.
entries.text: Effective strategy requires resilience in changing environments. Sustainable organisations distinguish between adapting execution and compromising purpose. They stay committed to their core objectives while responding wisely to changing circumstances.
entries.after: Navigation is what separates strategic leadership from operational management.

entries.title: Capability without intent.
entries.text: Capability without strategic intent produces a spectacular career and an unfinished assignment. Audit where the organisation’s most distinctive strength is being spent. If the answer is small wars it should never have entered, redirect that strength to the work the strategy was set to do.
entries.after: Can every team member describe our WHAT in one sentence?

entries.title: WHY before HOW.
entries.after: Do stakeholders believe and repeat our WHY?

entries.title: Benchmarking as strategy.
entries.text: One of the most dangerous instincts in a strategy room is the impulse to mimic peers. Benchmarking has its place. When “what everyone else is doing” becomes the dominant input, the organisation has stopped leading itself. List the three most recent strategic decisions and ask whether each came from your own theory of where this enterprise is going, or from a quiet wish to stop being conspicuously different.
entries.after: Do stakeholders believe and repeat our WHY?

entries.title: Symbol or substance.
entries.text: Some organisations bet on a symbol to do the work of substance: a hired name, a borrowed framework, a purchased certification. The hire is no substitute for the capability. Audit one initiative where the bet rests on a symbol, then shore up the substance or reduce the bet.
entries.after: between strategic ambition and current capability?

entries.title: Timing failures.
entries.text: Many strategic failures are failures of timing. The leader knew what to do and moved before the conditions favoured it. Identify one important move you are pushing early because you are anxious to resolve uncertainty. The same move made at the right moment is a different move.
entries.after: What signals tell us when to accelerate or pause?

entries.title: Built to a specification.
entries.text: The highest forms of organisational design are built to a specification that reflects a deep understanding of what the structure is meant to serve. Before you build, know exactly what you are building toward and why each element matters.

entries.title: Inherited boundaries.
entries.text: Existing categories can constrain strategic imagination. Markets, functions, customers, capabilities and partnerships may be understood through inherited assumptions that hide possibilities outside familiar boundaries. Ask: “What might become possible if one of our long-held assumptions about the boundaries of this opportunity is wrong?”

entries.title: Last season’s framework.
entries.text: Direction must be refreshed for the current season. The strategy that worked in the previous season needs review before it is applied to the next. Build the practice of seeking fresh direction before each major initiative.

entries.title: Destination and route.
entries.text: A common strategic failure is choosing the right goal and accepting a compromised route to reach it: a deal that delivers the number and burns the relationship, a hire that fits the seat and damages the team. Before the next material commitment, write the destination and the route on two separate lines and ask whether you would still defend the route if the outcome failed.
entries.after: If not — what must change?

entries.title: The common centre.
entries.text: Organisations that want to keep their core commitments coherent must resist fragmenting the practice of those commitments into locally adapted, individually customised forms that gradually lose their connection to the common centre.

entries.title: Structured into the rhythm.
entries.text: Organisations that want to serve their stakeholders consistently cannot leave that service to individual discretion. The most reliable provision is built into the institutional rhythm and does not depend on the surplus or the mood of the current leadership.

entries.title: Daily tending.
entries.text: Sustained organisational presence requires daily tending. Organisations that keep up the consistent daily act accumulate a depth of trust that occasional spectacular performance cannot replicate.
entries.after: Reviews happen only when there is a crisis.

entries.title: Values at the edges.
entries.text: The strongest cultural signal is how people are treated in the corridor, how decisions are made when no one is watching, and whether the language of the email matches the language of the boardroom. If stated values show up only in formal settings, the culture has not yet landed. Work on the small interactions at the edges and the centre will follow.
entries.after: The strategy exists in the boardroom but not on the floor.

entries.title: Surviving success.
entries.text: Leaders who build structures to survive scarcity and crisis, and none to survive abundance and success, have protected against the wrong threat. Organisations that collapse in prosperity forget what made the prosperity possible.
entries.after: the capabilities that make future success possible.

entries.title: The single measure.
entries.text: Whatever a team elevates above all else — speed, revenue, growth, reputation — will eventually be asked to deliver something it cannot. The test is whether the organisation has the honesty to see it when that happens.

entries.text: Organisations often rebuild structures without correcting the behaviours that caused the original failure. Recovery is temporary when the underlying assumptions, relationships and compromises remain unchanged.

entries.title: Substitution.
entries.text: Change requires more than removing a negative condition. A new operating pattern must replace the old one. Sustainable transformation is substitution.

entries.title: The mission in daily practice.
entries.text: An organisation that has articulated an extraordinary mission must answer a practical question: how does that mission live in daily practices, hiring decisions, budget allocations and conflict management? The high mission needs the daily practice that sustains it.

entries.title: Sound and communicable.
entries.text: A message creates value only if people can receive and understand it. Strategy must be both sound and communicable.

entries.title: Formula or practice.
entries.text: Mission statements repeated in meetings, values cited in performance reviews and brand language recycled in communications can become substitutes for the practice of what they claim. A formula that replaces the reality is more dangerous than the honest absence of either.
entries.after: written in the present tense of the future across all four dimensions.

entries.title: Shared meaning, shared action.
entries.text: Culture becomes powerful when people who share an institution also share its meaning and act on it together.

entries.title: I made this decision.
entries.text: Leaders who describe themselves as people to whom things happen have yet to take full ownership of their role. Ownership sounds like: “I made this decision and I own its results.”
